text: A notebook with one percent-percent-qsharp cell is fine for a tutorial. A real project needs an actual repository layout — one that keeps the quantum algorithm and the orchestration or analysis as clearly separate concerns, each testable and reusable on its own.

Four things to get right: a realistic repo layout for a Q#-plus-Python project. The qsharp.json manifest plus a src folder is the right boundary for the quantum library part — independently compilable, independently testable, independently resource-estimable, with no Python involved at all. Python code on the other side of that boundary stays decoupled from implementation details — it only needs operation names and signatures. And there's a real gotcha around recompilation timing worth knowing before it bites you.

Here's the shape: qsharp.json and src hold the reusable Q# operations — Oracles, Diffusion, Algorithms, each its own file. Experiments holds Python orchestration — parameter sweeps, result aggregation, plotting. Notebooks holds interactive exploration before code moves into src. This mirrors the operations-versus-functions discipline from Chapter 2, one level up: a reviewer can answer is this logic quantum or classical orchestration just by which folder they're looking in.

Once qsharp.init is pointed at the project root, operations defined anywhere under src become available to qsharp.run by their fully-qualified namespace name, exactly as if they'd been defined inline in a notebook cell. Namespaces matter here precisely because this is a multi-file project — Python refers to operations by their full namespace path, not by which file they happen to live in.

Inside an active qsharp.init session, editing a dot-q-s file under src and re-running a Python cell that calls into it triggers automatic recompilation — you don't need to manually rebuild first. The gotcha runs the other direction: a stale Python-side reference, a variable already holding a compiled callable from before the edit, may still point at the old version. When behavior doesn't match a file you just edited, re-running the Python call — not assuming the edit took effect everywhere — is the first thing to check.

Next lesson's lab puts this whole chapter together: write a Q# operation, call it many times from Python across this exact kind of project boundary, and validate the result against independently-derived theory.
